title: Misleading graphs
examples: How can a graph trick you into thinking something is true?
What should I look out for when I see a graph in the news?
Is it always true that a graph shows the whole story?

explain.say: Today we are learning about graphs that can be misleading. A graph is a great way to show data. But sometimes people make them look wrong.
One trick is using cut-off axes. This means the graph does not start at zero. It makes small changes look very big.
Another trick is cherry-picking data. This means only showing the data points that support one idea. They leave out the rest.
Always check the scale on the vertical axis. The scale should usually start at zero for a fair picture. This keeps the comparison honest.

draw.text: Check the vertical axis starts at zero.

explain.say: For a real-life example, think about tracking your height. If a graph only shows you growing between age ten and age twelve, it misses your growth before that.

draw.text: Real life: Tracking growth over time.

explain.say: A common mistake is assuming a graph shows the whole story. You must always ask what data is missing from the picture.

draw.text: Don't assume the graph is complete.

faq.q: Why are some graphs not starting at zero?
faq.a: Sometimes they do not start at zero to make small differences look bigger. This is a common trick to mislead the viewer.
asks: Does the axis have to start at zero?
Why do they cut off the bottom of the graph?

faq.q: What does 'cherry-picking' mean when talking about graphs?
faq.a: It means only choosing the best pieces of data to show. They leave out the data that tells a different story.
asks: What is the opposite of cherry-picking?

faq.q: How do I check if a graph is fair?
faq.a: You should check the scale on both the horizontal and vertical axes. Make sure the scale is consistent and starts at zero if it should.
asks: What should I look at first?

faq.q: If a graph shows temperature, does the scale always have to start at zero?
faq.a: No, for temperature, starting at zero might be fine, but for things like population change, it usually should start at zero.
asks: Is there an exception for temperature graphs?

faq.q: If I see a graph, what is the first thing I should do?
faq.a: The first thing you should do is look at the labels and the axes. Understand what the graph is measuring before looking at the lines.
asks: What is the best first step?
Should I read the title first?

facts: A graph's axes tell you what is being measured.
Starting an axis at zero gives the most accurate comparison.
Cherry-picking means selecting only favorable data points.
The scale must be consistent across the entire graph.

quiz.say: A graph shows sales increasing from 100 to 500, but the vertical axis starts at 80. What is the graph doing?

options.show: Comparing it to the previous year's sales
options.say: Comparing it to the previous year's sales

quiz.why: Because the axis cuts off the lower numbers, the jump looks much bigger than it really is.

wrong.0: This is wrong because the cut-off axis makes the growth look much faster.
wrong.2: This is wrong because the graph is not showing the true total if the axis is cut.
wrong.3: This is wrong because the graph only shows a small section of the data.

quiz.say: A graph shows student participation in three years: Year 1 (10 students), Year 2 (15 students), and Year 3 (100 students). If the graph only plots Year 2 and Year 3, what trick is used?
quiz.why: The creator chose to leave out Year 1 data to make the growth from Year 2 to Year 3 look more dramatic.

wrong.1: This is wrong because the axis itself is likely fine; the data points are just missing.
wrong.2: This is wrong because the numbers themselves are being selectively removed, not just the units.
wrong.3: This is wrong because the data points are not following a repeating pattern.

quiz.say: Which of these graph descriptions is the most honest representation of data?
quiz.show: Axis starts at zero, all data shown

options.show: A graph where the vertical axis starts at zero and includes all recorded years.
options.say: A graph where the vertical axis starts at zero and includes all recorded years.

options.show: A graph starting at 10 to make small rises look big.
options.say: A graph starting at 10 to make small rises look big.

options.show: A graph that only shows the highest numbers.
options.say: A graph that only shows the highest numbers.

options.show: A graph with unevenly spaced points.
options.say: A graph with unevenly spaced points.

quiz.why: Starting at zero and including all data gives the viewer the full, unbiased picture of what happened.

wrong.1: This is wrong because starting away from zero always exaggerates the change.
wrong.2: This is wrong because it hides the context of the lower numbers.
wrong.3: This is wrong because uneven spacing can confuse the rate of change.
